issues.legal_issue: A successor court may entertain a statutory petition to cancel a decree and is the proper court to receive the certificate where jurisdiction over such petitions passed to it and the prior decree is treated as its own order.
material_facts: An appellate decree was made by the Privy Council after its jurisdiction to entertain the appeal had ceased, under a transition that allowed it to dispose of the pending appeal.
The resulting decree was treated as an order of the Federal Court, and later as an order of the Supreme Court.
The petitioner sought cancellation of the decree on the basis of a Collector’s certificate addressed to the Supreme Court.
An earlier certificate had been held invalid because it was addressed to the executing court rather than the court that passed the decree; the new certificate was addressed to the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court could entertain the petition and was, in effect and substance, the court that passed the decree for the purpose of receiving the certificate. The certificate was valid, and the earlier decision did not bar the petition.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 5 and 8 of the Abolition of the Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949, the Federal Court acquired jurisdiction over relevant pending appeals and petitions, and an Order-in-Council had the effect of an order or decree of the Federal Court. Article 374(2) of the Constitution treated the Federal Court’s orders as orders of the Supreme Court, while Article 135 conferred on the Supreme Court the Federal Court’s relevant jurisdiction. Applying the principle in Rachapa v. Amingouda (1881) V Bom. 283 that a certificate must be addressed to the court that passed the decree, the Supreme Court held that the successor court was the proper addressee. The earlier ruling concerned a certificate addressed to the wrong court and did not preclude consideration of the new certificate.

rule.if: certificate_cancellation_proceeding and jurisdiction_over_such_petitions_passed_to_successor_court and prior_decree_treated_as_successor_court_order and certificate_addressed_to_successor_court and earlier_ruling_rejected_certificate_for_wrong_addressee

predicates.certificate_cancellation_proceeding: A person brought a proceeding seeking cancellation of a decree on the basis of an official certificate.
predicates.jurisdiction_over_such_petitions_passed_: Legal changes transferred jurisdiction over such petitions from a former appellate court to an intermediate court and then to the current court.
predicates.prior_decree_treated_as_successor_court_: Legal changes treated the former appellate court’s decree first as an order of an intermediate court and then as an order of the current court.
predicates.certificate_addressed_to_successor_court: The official who issued the new certificate addressed it to the current successor court.
predicates.earlier_ruling_rejected_certificate_for_: An earlier court rejected a certificate because it had been addressed to a court other than the court that passed the decree.

issues.definition: When a cancellation proceeding follows a transfer of jurisdiction, the decree is treated as an order of the successor court, and the new certificate is addressed to that court despite an earlier ruling about a certificate sent to the wrong court, the successor court may hear the proceeding and treat the certificate as valid.

issues.legal_issue: A court must cancel the part of a decree concerning protected office-remuneration property when a valid official certificate establishes that the property is covered by the statutory protection.
material_facts: The lands were recorded as part of a hereditary office and assigned as remuneration to its officiator.
The decree entitled the respondent to recover a share of the lands by partition, and the Collector’s certificate stated that the lands were inalienable and not liable to civil process.
The certificate was issued under the relevant statutory procedure and was confirmed on appeal to the revenue authority.
The parties did not dispute that the lands were governed by the Act or that a duly issued certificate made cancellation obligatory.
issues.conclusion: The decree was cancelled insofar as it operated on or included rights to the office and the watan lands identified in the certificate.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10 of the Bombay Hereditary Offices Act, 1874, requires the court, on receiving a certificate from the Collector stating the specified particulars, to cancel a decree insofar as it concerns watan property or its profits assigned as remuneration under section 23, where the property has passed or may pass under the decree to someone other than the officiator without government sanction. Once the certificate is duly issued and the property is covered by it, cancellation is obligatory.

predicates.decree_cancellation_proceeding: A person brought a proceeding seeking cancellation of a decree concerning particular property.
predicates.property_assigned_as_office_remuneration: The property was assigned as remuneration to the person holding a hereditary office.
predicates.decree_would_transfer_protected_property: The decree would cause the property or an interest in it to pass to someone other than the officeholder without the required government sanction.
predicates.valid_official_certificate_covers_proper: The Collector issued a valid certificate identifying the property as protected office-remuneration property.

issues.definition: If a decree-cancellation proceeding concerns property assigned as office remuneration, the decree would transfer it to another person without sanction, and a valid official certificate covers it, the decree must be cancelled as to that property.
